opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the uncomfortable truth is that we're in a pre-paradigmatic situation. We're like alchemists who've figured out that if you mix certain things and heat them, you get gunpowder. It works, it works reliably, and you can even get rough empirical laws about how much you put in and how big the bang is. But we don't have chemistry yet.

The scaling laws are real empirical regularities. You put in more compute, more data, more parameters, and the loss goes down in this remarkably smooth, predictable way. That's fascinating, and it tells you *something* deep is going on. My rough intuition is that the world has a lot of compressible structure, and these systems are very general-purpose machines for finding that structure, as long as you give them enough capacity and signal. Gradient descent on big, overparameterized networks turns out to be a much better search procedure than anyone expected. The old statistical learning theory said this should overfit and fall apart, and it just didn't.

But here's the part I want to emphasize. Predicting the *loss* is not the same as understanding the *system*. We can tell you roughly what the cross-entropy will be at the next order of magnitude. We cannot tell you what capabilities will emerge, what the model will actually do in novel situations, or what internal algorithms it's running. Those are the questions that actually matter, and on those we're basically flying blind.

So my interpretation isn't "scaling works, therefore we understand intelligence." It's closer to "scaling works, and that should scare us a bit." We're building increasingly powerful systems by turning a knob we don't understand, and the fact that the knob works so well means we're going to keep turning it faster than our understanding catches up. In any other engineering discipline, if you said "we have no theory of why this bridge stays up, but we keep making it taller and it hasn't fallen yet," people would rightly be alarmed.

That's why I care so much about interpretability and, more broadly, about building systems where we actually know what's going on inside. Not because scaling is fake, quite the opposite. Because it's real, and a lack of theory is a lack of control.

r001.rationale: The response compares scaling to alchemy and gunpowder, but does not compare it to biological brains growing larger and gaining new intellectual abilities.

r002.rationale: The response says scaling’s effects on loss are predictable and capabilities are not, but does not argue that lacking an explanation is no reason to predict when scaling’s benefits will stop.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing. I think the fact that we don't have a deep theory is actually the most important part of the story, not a footnote to it. We built these things empirically. Someone noticed that if you make the model bigger and feed it more data, the loss goes down, and it goes down in this eerily smooth, predictable way across many orders of magnitude. And then everyone just kept doing it. Nobody derived scaling laws from first principles and then went and built GPT. It was the other way around.

So how do I interpret it? Honestly, I think it's telling us something fairly humbling about intelligence. We spent decades assuming that intelligence was this very special, very structured thing that you'd need to carefully engineer, with the right inductive biases, the right symbolic machinery, whatever. And it turns out that if you take a pretty generic function approximator, point it at a huge chunk of the data humanity has produced, and apply enough compute, a lot of what we called intelligence just falls out. That's not a triumph of our understanding. It's more like we tripped over something.

And I'd argue the analogy to the history of science is pretty apt here. People were building steam engines long before thermodynamics existed. Carnot came along afterwards to explain why they worked. We're at the steam engine stage. The difference is that a steam engine that you don't understand can explode and kill a few people in a factory. A system that is approaching or exceeding human-level cognition that you don't understand is a very different kind of object to be ignorant about.

So from my perspective, the lack of theory is not merely an intellectual gap. It means we cannot predict what capabilities will emerge at the next scale. We can predict the loss curve, which is remarkable, but the loss is a proxy. It doesn't tell you when a model learns to do in-context learning, or write exploits, or model the person it's talking to. Those things show up as surprises, and the people building these systems will openly tell you they were surprised. And I don't think "we don't know why it works, but it keeps working, so let's keep going" is a stance you'd accept in any other engineering discipline that deals with something this powerful.

There's a deeper point too. I think the reason we lack a theory is that we don't actually have a good theory of intelligence or of what these models are internally. Interpretability is making real progress, but it's miles behind capabilities. We're in the position of a biologist who can breed organisms with whatever traits they want but can't read the genome. You can get very far that way. You can also get very far in a direction you really didn't intend.

So I guess my short answer is: the success of scaling should make you less confident in our mastery of this technology, not more. The empirical result is real, it's incredible, and it's also precisely the reason I think we should be a lot more careful than we're currently being.

r001.rationale: The response compares scaling to steam engines and to breeding organisms without reading their genomes. It does not compare scaling to new intellectual abilities emerging as biological brains grow.

r002.rationale: The response says we cannot predict what capabilities will emerge at the next scale, but it does not argue that ignorance of why scaling works fails to justify predicting when its benefits will stop.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to take the empirical results seriously. We have this recipe: make the network bigger, give it more data, spend more compute, and it gets better at a remarkably broad range of things. Our inability to fully explain that doesn’t make the observation less real. It means our theory hasn’t caught up.

But there are different levels of understanding here. Being able to predict that the loss will improve is useful. It doesn’t mean you understand what algorithm the model has learned, what capabilities will emerge, or how it will behave in a situation very different from its training data. You can have a fairly predictable training process that produces a system whose behavior is much harder to predict.

So I take scaling as evidence that relatively simple learning procedures can produce much more general capabilities than we might have expected. I don’t take it as proof that the current recipe will work forever. But I’m also very skeptical of the argument that there must be some imminent barrier just because we don’t have a satisfying theory. Nature doesn’t owe us an explanation before something works. And, especially from a safety perspective, we shouldn’t assume that understanding will necessarily arrive before capability.

r001.rationale: The response discusses broader capabilities from scaling, but does not compare this to new intellectual abilities emerging as biological brains grow.

r002.rationale: It rejects predicting an imminent scaling barrier solely because we lack a satisfying theory, while acknowledging that scaling may not work forever.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should take the empirical result seriously, even if we don’t have a satisfying theory. We found that you can take a fairly general learning algorithm, give it more compute and more data, and it learns increasingly sophisticated things. That’s a remarkable fact about the world. Our inability to explain it doesn’t make it less real.

But there’s a big difference between knowing how to make a system more capable and understanding what you’ve made. You can predict that the loss will improve without being able to predict every capability that will appear, or how the system will behave in a situation you haven’t tested.

So I see scaling as evidence that relatively simple methods can produce very general capabilities. I don’t see it as evidence that those capabilities will automatically be understandable or controllable. And that gap is precisely what worries me: we’re getting better at building these systems much faster than we’re getting better at understanding them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses increasingly sophisticated capabilities from more compute and data, but it does not compare scaling to new intellectual abilities emerging as biological brains grow.

r002.rationale: The response says lack of explanation does not make scaling less real, but it does not argue that this ignorance prevents predicting when scaling’s benefits will stop.
